meaningMnemonic: See the energy bursting outward? That's an explosion . Boom!
The three lines that make up the river radical are being warped to the left here. Probably by a massive force of rushing water, because this is a flood . RUN!

This radical is pretty complicated, but not much looks like this radical, so you're in luck. This looks like a giant flying airship of some kind. See the propellers on the back as it moves to the left? Just imagine a kind of steampunk airship like this flying through the air. That's why this radical is fly — because it's flying.

This radical looks like a mole . Picture its head poking out of a pile of dirt and looking up to the sky, whiskers twitching. Alternately, here's a mnemonic: What lives under the ground in private places covered in dirt? A mole! Sure, its walls, ceiling, and floors are all dirt, but that's what home is to a mole.

This radical looks like a combination of the brush radical ( 聿 ) and the beauty kanji ( 美 ). So what's something beautiful painted with a brush? The most famous example is probably the Mona Lisa . This Mona Lisa just happens to have some horns sketched on… by you. Oh, hey, you've just vandalized the Mona Lisa. Nice one.

The horns on the king give him an ego. Which in turn gives him a sense of righteousness . He shouldn't act all righteous like that, but I suppose it's what kings do. If you had horns and a big ego, you'd probably think you were the epitome of righteousness too.

You have an outfit valley , which is a valley where you store your abundant number of outfits. Yes, you're so wealthy that not only can you purchase a valley for yourself, you can also afford to use it like a walk-in closet. Hints See the green mountains rising on either side of the valley, hear the birdsong in the distance… and behold the miles of clothes racks that hold all your outfits. This valley is the only space big enough to contain your material abundance and wealth.
readingMnemonic: This valley is also abundant with wealthy you ths ( ゆう ) — trendy, wealthy youths who come from around the world to descend on your valley and peep your outfit collection. Hints Picture these wealthy youths as they peruse your valley of outfits. They're mostly influencers making short-form video content for their socials, basically leeching off your abundance. Ugh. Is this how people get wealthy in the 21st century?

meaningMnemonic: You take some flag s, nine in total, and put them one by one up your butt . Hints Imagine taking these nine flags... count 'em... and putting them up your butt. With each one that's up there it gets harder and harder to fit the next one in.
readingMnemonic: Now that you have nine flags inside your butt , you have to get them out. But, you don't know how to. So you ask Siri ( しり ), "How do I get nine flags out of my butt?" Hints In your head, doing the Siri voice, come up with an answer for your nine-flags-in-the-butt predicament.

meaningMnemonic: You take a stone to the forehead of a turkey . It is certain that you will damage it. Hints Try hitting a sponge on a turkey's forehead. Not certain. Now a stone. Certain .
readingMnemonic: You're killing this turkey, and you need to make sure he's dead for certain . The reason you need to make sure this turkey is dead is because of the cock ( かく ) in your life. Male chickens get really jealous when turkeys are around. Hints As you smash the stone into the turkey's forehead, yell out "This is for you, my cock! THIS IS FOR YOU!" Your cock lover watches from the shadows.

meaningMnemonic: Under a tree a drunkard sits with twenty little contraptions . There's little electronic ones, little bopping ones, little walking ones... twenty of them. Hints Can you even imagine twenty completely unique contraptions? Why don't you try, just for fun.
readingMnemonic: You want to know what these contraptions are for, so you ask. The drunkard says, "These are kay ak ( かい ) contraptions *urp* they're for your uh *blarp* kayak... things." Hints "Kayak contraptions" is pretty vague, but you do have a kayak, so you're tempted anyway. If only you could figure out what each contraption did so you could justify buying some.

meaningMnemonic: That outfit on your skin is there to cover you up. In polite society, it's expected that you cover your skin with some kind of outfit — even if you have to wear something that causes you to incur damage, like circulation-cutting skinny jeans or a shirt with a really scratchy tag. Hints Imagine the most uncomfortable outfit you can. Your body is incurring some minor damage right now, but hey — at least you're covering your skin properly.
readingMnemonic: Another reason to cover yourself is to retain he at ( ひ ). Actually, retaining heat and staying warm is probably the reason people started covering themselves up in the first place. Hints Even if you incur some damage from uncomfortable clothing, it's better to cover up and retain heat than to underdress and incur damage from frostbite or something.

meaningMnemonic: In the animal kingdom, a snake is the most likely to commit a crime . Remember the Garden of Eden? The snake was the bad guy. Ever since then, snakes are the animal most known for committing crimes. Hints Picture a snake as a hardened criminal. See this snake with many prison tattoos and muscles from working out in his jail cell. Hear the snake hissing as it slithers about to commit yet another crime.
readingMnemonic: This snake has evaded the law for too long. It’s time for a true hero to put an end to its crime spree. Enter Han ( はん ) Solo. Han Solo is the only man strong and brave enough to put an end to this snake and his crime filled ways. Hints Now see Han Solo doing battle with the snake (cue Star Wars music). The snake hisses and lunges at Han, but Han shoots the snake and it’s incapacitated. Smell the smell of scorched snake flesh in your nose.

meaningMnemonic: You slip off the roof and bang up your rib cage and mouth . Oof, that's some serious damage . How will you explain this injury to your pals at the We Never Fall Off of Roofs Club? Hints Imagine the moment you fall off the roof. In slow motion you can see the roof moving away, then BAM! You've injured your rib cage and mouth. Ow! If only you were a video game character that never takes fall damage.
readingMnemonic: As you try to assess the damage , you hear someone shout " Guy ( がい )! Hey, you okay, guy?" They run up to you, but your rib cage and mouth are too damaged for you to respond. "Okay guy, just hang in there, guy. I'm gonna get you to the hospital and we'll treat that injury , guy." Hints "Don't worry, my guy," your rescuer says. "I'm gonna call up those paramedic guys, and they're gonna get you in to see one of those doctor guys right away. You just hang in there, big guy!"

meaningMnemonic: What you say is righteousness , at least that's what you believe. You keep talking and saying these things, and you don't listen to anyone else's words. This is your style of deliberation and discussion . Hints Picture yourself in a deliberation with some other people. They think what they're saying is right, and it drives you mad. Then you realize that you're doing the same thing.
readingMnemonic: What are you in deliberation about? Whether or not to send some poor soul to the gui llotine ( ぎ ). "I think he should go," you say. "I don't think he should," says another. This deliberation is going nowhere... Hints Imagine how the deliberation concludes. Then, at the end, someone says "This deliberation is over! We have decided to _________" (in regards to the guillotine).

meaningMnemonic: A Chinese turkey is difficult to find because they are so rare. Chinese turkeys are the rarest variety of turkey, so naturally, finding one is exceedingly difficult. Hints Try and picture a Chinese turkey in your brain. Now imagine yourself trying to catch it, but you just can’t. It’s too difficult. The Chinese turkey is too elusive.
readingMnemonic: Do you know the actual reason Chinese turkey are so difficult to find? It’s because they’re all made out of Naan ( なん ). Of course they’re elusive when they blend in so well with all the other Naan! Hints Picture yourself entering a bakery, frantically scouring through all the Naan in an attempt to find one that’s actually a Chinese turkey. "WHERE ARE THE TURKEYS?", you scream, to everyone else’s bewilderment. Those elusive, difficult to find Chinese Naan turkeys…

meaningMnemonic: A flood and a fire ! At the same time? This is a disaster ! Hints Imagine a disaster so bad that there are floods AND fires. That's too much!
readingMnemonic: This disaster was caused by your cy borg ( さい )! It's malfunctioning, running around leaking large amounts of water and breathing fire. I guess you didn't work out all the kinks before you let it roam wild. Hints You better figure out a way to stop your cyborg from causing more disasters like this. Fix it now, or you're gonna be in big trouble.

meaningMnemonic: When a woman sees the Mona Lisa , she feels a strong feeling of dislike . All women dislike the Mona Lisa because of how much attention she gets. Hints Imagine yourself feeling this strong dislike towards the Mona Lisa. She gets all the attention and you get none. It’s not fair and you’re upset.
readingMnemonic: You dislike the Mona Lisa so much you hire Ken ( けん ) the samurai to cut her up. Hints Ken walks slowly toward the Mona Lisa, dislike shines in his eyes, but then! He falls for her too. No! Ken, destroy her!

meaningMnemonic: If you put your mouth on a tree and try to eat it, you’re probably a distressed and troubled individual (unless you’re a woodchuck). You don’t need to eat this tree, you have plenty of food at home. Get your mouth off that tree you distressed child. Hints Imagine yourself as this distressed and troubled person. Taste the taste of sap and bark in your mouth as you nom on the tree with all your might.
readingMnemonic: You thought you were the most distressed and troubled person in this situation, but then you look up and see a very equally distressed and troubled con dor ( こん ). The tree you've been mouthing is its home. And now you've slobbered all over it, ruining this condor's day. Hints Picture a very distressed condor watching you munch your mouth all over its tree house. You've made a condor enemy this day.

meaningMnemonic: A flowers net is upon your forehead in the evening . These appear on your head at night whenever you are having a dream . Hints Watch yourself sleeping. Then, a net of flowers appear on your forehead as you start to dream.
readingMnemonic: You dream about cows saying " moo ( む ), moo, moo!" Hints While still dreaming, you say "moo" out loud too. "Moooo!"

meaningMnemonic: Rain causes a landslide that causes an earthquake !!! The earth doesn't just slide, it shake s and quake s. Hints Picture this happening in real time. First it starts to rain really hard, then the ground starts to shift and run, then everything is shaking and quaking so violently it's an earthquake!
readingMnemonic: The earthquake shakes you so violently that you fall over, banging your shin ( しん ) on the coffee table. The edge of the coffee table is very sharp, so it cuts into your shin pretty badly. Hints You grab your shin, but the earthquake shakes the coffee table toward you to hit your shin yet again! Ow ow ow stop!

meaningMnemonic: A narwhal sticks a stick into the dirt to see what might exist underneath it. Narwhals live in the sea, you see. So they're convinced nothing can exist anywhere else. Hints Imagine seeing a narwhal sticking a stick, and maybe even its horn too, into the dirt on land. It needs to know if life exists outside of the ocean for sure.
readingMnemonic: The narwhal can't find anything but it can't stop thinking about what could exist outside of its world. It pulls out a xy lophone ( ざい ) and starts tapping the keys with its horn. It plays a sad song about the meaning of life and whether existence is worth it. Hints Hear the plinky plink of the xylophone and think about what exists in this world. It's a sad song, you realize.

meaningMnemonic: The fly radical and the fly kanji are exactly the same! Awesome! Hints Thanks to that radical knowledge, you're flying through these kanji now.
readingMnemonic: When you fly , you generate a lot of he at ( ひ ) because you're moving so fast through the atmosphere. Normally this heat would be a nuisance, but you're a superhero so it doesn't bother you. This is actually the reason you're able to fly — you're a superhero and super resistant to heat. Hints You're flying through the air super fast. Feel the air rushing past you as heat builds up all over your body from rocketing through the air so fast.

meaningMnemonic: You stand on the Cliff of Life and give birth to a child. Oh no! You’re standing too close to the edge of the Cliff of Life! The baby falls off the cliff right after you give birth to it! In your despair, you throw all your property off the cliff too. Hints The baby is falling off the cliff! Imagine the sheer terror you feel as the baby plummets towards the ground below.
readingMnemonic: You give birth , and now this happens. Such bad luck. But wait! What's that sound? Sleigh bells? Could it be?! It's San ta-san ( さん )! He caught your baby! And all your property . Hints Oh Santa-san. You're always here for me when I need you most. You can keep all my property and give it away as presents.

meaningMnemonic: Put a net around a criminal to show their guilt . Criminals look like anyone else on the street, so you decide to tie them in nets to make sure people know who they're dealing with. Hints Imagine throwing a net around someone you think, no, you know is guilty of doing something bad to you. It feels pretty nice.
readingMnemonic: The guilt shows on the criminal's face. They smile, shrug, and pull a stolen xy lophone ( ざい ) out of their back pocket. Hints Woah! The xylophone is huge, how did they... well whatever, you definitely have proof that they're guilty now and the cops should be here any minute to take your criminal catch.

meaningMnemonic: The leader 's mouth has grown old from saying so many things. This is what makes them different from everyone else, they speak truly like an individual . Hints Imagine that leader's old mouth saying things that make them stand apart from the others. They're individual from everyone else.
readingMnemonic: As an individual , they must teach all the 子 s ( こ ) their way. Their individual way. Hints "You must be your own individual. Don't be sheeple," he says to the 子 s.

meaningMnemonic: Next to a tree , you spot poop , not once but twice. Only a drunkard would be the type of person to not use the nearby machine toilet. There's a perfectly good outhouse with a machine toilet right there, but this drunkard is so drunk that he decides to poop under the tree instead. And not only does he poop once, he poops twice. Hints Imagine this drunkard, squatting down under the tree to poop. You can smell the poop and a faint stench of alcohol in the air. How could he not have realized that there was a machine toilet right there?
readingMnemonic: Oh, I see — the door to the outhouse with the machine toilet is locked, and the drunkard doesn't have the key ( き ). If he had a machine like a jackhammer, or a circular saw, or some other heavy duty machine, he might be able to get in without a key, but since he has none of those or a key, he's reduced to pooping under the tree instead. Hints Listen to the drunkard grumbling about the lack of a key as he poops under the tree. He doesn't sound happy, and every time he stresses to push out the poop, his voice fluctuates. Imagine hearing this in your mind and being a wee bit disgusted.

meaningMnemonic: Someone stabbed the leader mole with a knife to overthrow it. Now there is a new mole leader. Because that's what happens when you overthrow someone—someone else needs to take over. In this case, a vengeful mole. Hints Imagine a mole sneaking up behind the leader mole and stabbing him with a knife. This type of overthrowing of leadership feels familiar to you. Maybe this has happened before in the past?
readingMnemonic: Where do leaders get overthrow n the most? In とう きょう . Just think back in Japanese history, back when everyone was at war with one another. People were taking over and getting overthrown and then that guy gets overthrown and then THAT guy gets overthrown. Basically, it used to be hard to stay a leader in とうきょう . Hints Picture this like an exaggerated reenactment on the History channel. Leader after leader of とうきょう gets overthrown and replaced with the next guy. It never stops. (Until the end of the Edo period, I guess.)

meaningMnemonic: Tying a thread to a tombstone each year will help you manage the passage of time . That way you’ll know how many years you pass through , since you’ll have one thread for each year to count. Hints Picture yourself coming back to the same tombstone each passing year and tying a new thread to it. You're trying to manage these feelings by keeping track of how much time passes.
readingMnemonic: Dealing with the passage of time can be tough, so after you tie the thread to the tombstone, each year you eat a piece of ca ke ( けい ). You already eat cake to mark the passage of time on your birthday, so why not here as well? Hints Maybe this is your future tombstone, and eating cake each year is a preemptive celebration of your death day! Ooh, what a spooky theory.

meaningMnemonic: Sitting on the lid of a toilet, you're praying your poop explosion will be flushed away, beseeching the cross decorating the bathroom wall. The poop needs to be one hundred percent flushed away because you're on a date, and you don't want even one percent of your explosion left for them to see. Hints You take a peek under the lid to check, and your poop explosion is one hundred percent gone! Phew!
readingMnemonic: It was extra important that there was zero percent poop left, because you're not on a date just anywhere, you're at the Ritz ( りつ )! Hints Look around you at the classy surroundings of the Ritz Hotel bathroom. You feel one hundred percent relieved now, and ready to enjoy your date at the Ritz!

meaningMnemonic: Under any cliff , there's some dirt that's under a lot of pressure . Hints Imagine being down there under that heavy cliff. Imagine feeling the cliff's pressure as you watch it compress the dirt. It's so hard to breathe... h... help!
readingMnemonic: You want to increase the pressure , so you stack on a second cliff. " Ah, two ( あつ )?!" the dirt cries out in dismay. This dirt is tough, but it's really starting to feel the pressure now. Hints Imagine yelling out to the dirt to encourage it: "Ah, two cliffs is nothing! Come on, you got this!" You're the dirt's gym buddy, and you won't let it buckle under the pressure.

meaningMnemonic: If there is a building in the direction you want to go it will prevent you from going any further. Like, come on kid, you think you can just walk right through a building? Don't make me laugh! Hints There's a building right there. Try to go that direction. Oh, did the building prevent you? Told you so.
readingMnemonic: The building is prevent ing you from going the right direction, so you pull a bow ling ( ぼう ) ball out of your bag, aim, and bowl the building over. The building, and all the ones around it, go tumbling down. But now the rubble is preventing you from going further. Hints Your bowling antics are now preventing a bunch of people from going the directions they want to go. Nice job.

meaningMnemonic: You walk into this tree and hit your head on it, then a knife falls out of it to stab you. Ow! What the heck?! What was a knife doing in that tree? Hints Imagine the pain and confusion of being stabbed by a violent tree. You hit your head on the tree again, as if to test it, and again a knife falls out and stabs you. Oh, so it's a stabbing tree, is it? That does it.
readingMnemonic: There's nothing more dangerous than a tree that likes to stab , so you get your saw ( さ ) and start to saw it down. Trees that stab get sawed. Hints Feel the grain of the saw's wooden handle in your bare hand. As the saw bites into tree bark, a retaliatory rain of knives comes stabbing down around you. But you don't even flinch. You will saw this stabbing tree down.

meaningMnemonic: Wash your self with a big bar of soap if you're stinking everything up. Hints Seriously. If you or someone else is stinking to high heaven, embrace a big bar of self care.
readingMnemonic: You're stinking up the room because you spent your day rolling in 草 ( くさ ). And based on this particular stench, I'd say an animal left something in that 草 too... Hints Imagine trying to use a big bar of soap on yourself to get the stinky 草 off. But it's not working... the 草 stink is SO STRONG!

meaningMnemonic: Regardless of whether or not you wear a hat while you jackhammer , you’re going to have a surplus of noise. Jackhammers are loud, and your hat is doing nothing to dampen the racket. There’s a surplus of commotion coming from the jackhammer and onlookers are not amused. Hints The hat you’re wearing is ridiculous, giving you a surplus of bad style. Imagine a bunch of people scowling at you, not only because of your crazy hat, but because of the annoying sound of the jackhammer. Hear the obnoxious noise around you as the jackhammer rattles your bones.
readingMnemonic: One of the people walking by is the owner of a push cart yo -yo ( よ ) stand. Having a surplus of yo-yos, he starts throwing them at you. This makes you stop using the jackhammer as you need both hands to fend off the yo-yo barrage. Hints Your hat is doing little to defend you from the onslaught of yo-yos being tossed at you. Feel the yo-yos hitting your body and listen to them roll away after striking you.

meaningMnemonic: You see a flag stuck in the ground with a little bit of fur coming out from it and on closer inspection you realize it’s actually a tail . Someone stuck a flag into some sort of animal, pushing it under the ground. All that’s visible now is some fur and part of the tail. Hints What kind of animal could it be? You start to feel the soft fur with your hand and then the stench of death hits your nostrils. Ew.
readingMnemonic: You try to pull the flag out of the ground and hear a rumbling buzzing sound. At the end of the flagpole you see a huge bee hive ( び )! These bees made their home under the tail ! Maybe that’s why the flag was sticking in it… to warn people. Oops. Hints See the bees swarming out from around the tail and toward your face. Run! Run before there’s nothing left of you but your own tail!

meaningMnemonic: You say , throwing your hat on the ground in front of the bookshelf , "I have a theory !" All this reading and thinking has finally given you a wonderful idea, a theory you think might solve all of your problems! Hints This theory you've thought of is great, it's going to change everything!
readingMnemonic: "What is your theory, Ron ( ろん )?" asks Hermione. You're Ron Weasley, and you just came up with a theory that you think will help you stop Voldemort. Hints "Ron? Ron, what's your theory? What's your theory, Ron?" Hermione asks over and over. But you freeze. You don't remember who you are. "Hermione, I have a theory that I was just a person learning Japanese, and not a magical boy at all." "Shut up Ron, that's a stupid theory," she replies.

meaningMnemonic: Hanging off the edge of a cliff is a sun -worshipping child with a thick unibrow. Hanging off the cliff, the child cries out to the sun to save them from this cruel fate. Even the thickness of their unibrow is not enough to give the child the strength to climb back up on their own. Hints I mean, this unibrow is really, really thick. So thick it doesn’t even look real. But it is. It’s really real and really thick.
readingMnemonic: The child glances up at their thick unibrow and yells, " ah, two ( あつ )!" Yup, it turns out the sun misunderstood the child's pleas for help. Instead of pulling them up from the cliff, it gave them a second thick unibrow on top of the first one. Hints Imagine the sun noticing its mistake and apologizing to the child. "Ah, two thick unibrows wasn't what you wanted? Wow, I'm sorry. This is embarrassing… I'm actually not sure I can remove the second one now that it's on there."

meaningMnemonic: You place a cross on a Wolverine woman . She's gone now, but she was once your wife . Hints Oh, how you miss your Wolverine woman and her long, sharp claws… Now all you've got left to remember her by is this cross. Your poor, poor wife.
readingMnemonic: Wait a minute… She can't be dead because your wife is a cy borg ( さい )! How could you forget?! Hints All your wife needs is a little cyborg tune-up. Bionic brain here, some new claws there. Yep, your cy-wife's as good as new.

You use it when you hear a thought or viewpoint that really resonates with you — you totally agree with this person's take and feel exactly the same way. Preach!

sentences.english: My father teaches anthropology at the university.

sentences.japanese: この本を書いたのは日本で人類学を学んだモンゴル人の方だそうです。

meaningMnemonic: There is much deliberation and theory exchanging when you are trying to present an argument . Of course, it's a very nice one. Lots of thinking and stuff, you know? That's why there's deliberation and theories instead of just screaming. That kind of "argument."
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 私はその議論には意味がないと思ってるんですが、あなたはどんなご意見をお持ちですか？
sentences.english: I see no point in that argument, what is your opinion?

sentences.japanese: 今日はネットで議論されてる車イスユーザーの話題についてみんなで考えてみましょう。
sentences.english: Let's all think about the topic of wheelchair users being discussed on the Internet today.

sentences.japanese: コウイチとビエトは、夕飯に何を食べるかについて議論に議論を重ねました。

meaningMnemonic: If someone overthrow s your property , it'll end in bankruptcy . Without property you're sure to go bankrupt , unfortunately.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 父さんの会社の倒産のニュース、見たよ！
sentences.english: Father, I saw the news about your company's bankruptcy!

sentences.english: When I learned my company would go bankrupt, I looked up at the sky and saw a beautiful contrail.

meaningMnemonic: Check the pressure of your blood . It's your blood pressure .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: うちの家族はみんな血圧が高いんです。
sentences.english: Everyone in my family has high blood pressure.

sentences.japanese: 私は高血圧なので、血圧下げる薬を服用しています。

sentences.japanese: 低血圧だから朝起きられなくて困っているんです。今日は血圧をはかってもらったら、上が85で下が30でした。コウイチ先生、何とかしてもらえませんか？
sentences.english: I am having trouble getting up in the morning because I have low blood pressure. When I had my blood pressure taken today, it was eighty-five over thirty. Can you do something for me, Dr. Koichi?

meaningMnemonic: Remember how 手 can mean "doer" in some words? So here, you have borrow doer , or more simply borrower . This word is often used to specifically refer to borrowers in contrast to lenders.
readingMnemonic: You'll want to know the words 借りる and 手 to be able to read this one. Combine them to know the reading.

sentences.japanese: あのマンションは、お化けが出るというウワサのせいで借り手がつかない。
sentences.english: That apartment still doesn’t have any tenants because it’s rumored to be haunted.

sentences.japanese: 借り手は、銀行の金利が上がってほしくありません。
sentences.english: Borrowers do not want bank interest rates to rise.

sentences.japanese: そうは言っても、借り手が見つからない可能性もありますよね？
sentences.english: Regardless of what you say, there's still a possibility that we won't be able to find a tenant, right?

meaningMnemonic: A bow and an arrow . Put them together and you have a bow and arrow .
readingMnemonic: The reading is the vocab readings, 弓 and 矢 , put together. This is probably because this word is like two separate words put together, thus the "and" in the middle of the English translation.

sentences.japanese: このアイヌのダンスでは弓矢が使われます。
sentences.english: Bows and arrows are used in this Ainu dance.

sentences.japanese: このゲームでは、いつも弓矢を選んでプレイします。
sentences.english: In this game, I always choose to play with a bow and arrow.

sentences.japanese: 夏休みに父と山で竹の弓矢を作りました。
sentences.english: I made bamboo bows and arrows in the mountains with my father during summer vacation.

meaningMnemonic: The お is just there to be nice to your butt. This word simply means butt (or any other word for it, like buttocks or bottom ).
readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.

sentences.japanese: お尻にイボができました。
sentences.english: I got a wart on my buttocks.

sentences.japanese: 高いところに行くと、お尻がかゆくなるんです。
sentences.english: When I go to high places, my butt itches.

sentences.japanese: これはお尻のインナーマッスルのエクササイズです。
sentences.english: This is an exercise for the inner muscles of the buttocks.

meaningMnemonic: This is an adverb, but it has the same meaning (basically) as the kanji. It means certainly , and it can also mean surely .
readingMnemonic: The reading for this one is certainly weird. To remember the reading for this word, just think how you're certain that if you s tash ( たし ) the treasure, nobody will find it here.

sentences.japanese: それは確かにそうですね。
sentences.english: That is certainly true.

sentences.japanese: 彼は確かにリーダーに向いていると思います。でも、時々言葉がきついのがネックです。
sentences.english: He is certainly a good leader. But the problem is that sometimes his language is too harsh.

sentences.japanese: コウイチが百メートルほど飛ぶのを、この目で確かに見ました。
sentences.english: I'm certain I saw Koichi fly about one hundred meters with my own eyes.

meaningMnemonic: The person in charge of long discussion s is the chairman , or the speaker . They also say who gets to talk and for how long.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: 議長、今日の議題は何ですか？
sentences.english: Mr. Chairman, what is today's agenda?

sentences.japanese: その議長は、いつも皆の意見を公平に聞いてくれます。
sentences.english: That chairman always listens to everyone's opinions fairly.

sentences.japanese: 今、2024年の最初のFOMCでのパウエル議長の会見のビデオを見ているところです。
sentences.english: I am just now watching the video of Chairman Powell's press conference at the first FOMC meeting of 2024.

meaningMnemonic: A room where you meet for discussion s is known as a conference room .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: 会議室は三階にあります。
sentences.english: The conference room is located on the third floor.

sentences.japanese: この会議室にはプロジェクターとホワイトボードがあります。
sentences.english: This meeting room has a projector and whiteboard.

sentences.japanese: ビエトとコウイチが会議室に入ったまんまずっと出てこないんだ。
sentences.english: Viet and Koichi went in the meeting room and still haven't come out.

meaningMnemonic: A hole child isn't some kind of creepy hole child (not sure how else to describe it). It's a conger eel , a type of tasty eel eaten in Japan. It might be easier to learn the reading first, though, and use that, because the second meaning option is anago , the Japanese word for it (also used in English).
readingMnemonic: The reading is the two kun'yomi vocab readings combined. So, 穴 and 子 to combine make あなご . Just watch out for rendaku, which changes the reading of 子 from こ to ご .

sentences.japanese: 今日はお昼に穴子の天ぷらを食べました。
sentences.english: Today I had conger eel tempura for lunch.

sentences.japanese: 穴子の身はやわらかくて、食べやすいです。
sentences.english: The flesh of anago is soft and easy to eat.

sentences.japanese: アメリカでは穴子は手に入りにくいので、代わりにウナギが使われています。
sentences.english: Since it is difficult to get conger eel in America, freshwater eel is used instead.

meaningMnemonic: Throat candy is the kind of candy that should make your throat feel better. That's right, it's a cough drop or a throat lozenge . Don't just eat regular candy when your throat hurts! Use the right kind.
readingMnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi readings for both kanji. You've learned them both already, so you should be able to read this already!

sentences.japanese: 喉飴持ってない？
sentences.english: Do you happen to have a throat lozenge?

sentences.japanese: 今日はカゼを治すために、水分とって喉飴なめて、一日ゆっくりします。
sentences.english: Today, I will take water and lozenges to cure my cold, and then take it easy for the rest of the day.

sentences.japanese: 喉飴って理科室みたいな味がすると思わない？
sentences.english: Don't you think cough drops taste like the science room?

meaningMnemonic: Even in the middle of your dream you're thinking about your body pillows. You're crazy about them, wrapped in absorption . Alternatively, this describes doing something frantic ally, like running away from somebody or something.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 彼女はゲームに夢中になっていて、彼の声が聞こえませんでした。
sentences.english: She was so engrossed in the game that she did not hear him.

sentences.japanese: テレビドラマに夢中になっていて、夕食の準備を忘れていました。
sentences.english: I was so engrossed in a TV drama that I forgot to prepare dinner.

sentences.japanese: そのウェイトレスは、彼女に夢中になっている皿洗いの男に追いかけられ、とにかく夢中で家まで走って帰りました。
sentences.english: The waitress, pursued by a dishwasher smitten with her, ran home frantically.

meaningMnemonic: You have crime and you have guilt . Sounds like you did the crime .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: イジメは犯罪ですよ。
sentences.english: Bullying is a crime.

sentences.japanese: 日本の学校では、先生の犯罪歴をチェックしないんですか？

sentences.japanese: 日本で一番重い犯罪は何か知っていますか？
sentences.english: Do you know what the most serious crime in Japan is?

meaningMnemonic: A dangerous machine is walking through your town, destroying everything. This is a huge crisis !
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 日本は今、国家存亡の危機にあります。
sentences.english: Japan is currently facing a crisis that threatens its national survival.

sentences.japanese: もうちょっと危機感もった方がいいんじゃない？
sentences.english: Maybe you should have a bit more sense of urgency.

sentences.japanese: 第三次世界大戦は文明の危機につながります。
sentences.english: World War III will lead to a crisis of civilization.

meaningMnemonic: A difficult injustice to take from someone is a criticism . Ugh, what a pain to be criticized! So difficult, and besides, it's an injustice, because I'm perfect!
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: その記事の内容には、たくさんの非難の声が上がりました。
sentences.english: The article received a lot of flak for its content.

sentences.japanese: あの行動に非難の目を向ける人が多くて、ビックリしました。
sentences.english: I was surprised at how many people were condemning that behavior.

sentences.japanese: ちょっとしたイタズラのつもりだったのに、その若者は世間の非難にさらされることになってしまいました。
sentences.english: What was meant to be a minor prank ended up exposing the young man to public condemnation.

meaningMnemonic: A crime person is a culprit , or a criminal . Just note that 犯人 is mostly used to talk about the culprit of a specific crime, not criminals in general.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: クッキー食べた犯人、お父さんだった。
sentences.english: The culprit who ate the cookies turned out to be Dad.

sentences.japanese: まだ犯人つかまってないらしいよ。
sentences.english: I heard they haven't caught the culprit yet.

sentences.japanese: その犯人は、口は災いの元だということを思い知った。
sentences.english: The criminal learned the hard way that speaking carelessly can bring disaster.

meaningMnemonic: When you get cover ed in damage , you can't avoid it — you really suffer damage . 被害 refers to damage or harm that someone suffers because of some unfortunate occurrence, like a crime, accident, or disaster. As the kanji 被 suggests, it emphasizes being on the receiving end of the harm, not just the damage itself. You'll mostly see it in serious contexts where victims or losses are being discussed — news articles and official reports, for example.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: この町は、山火事の被害は受けませんでした。
sentences.english: This town wasn't damaged by the wildfire.

sentences.japanese: 被害にあった方がガマンしなきゃいけないなんて、おかしいよ！
sentences.english: It's not right that the victim has to be the one to endure it!

sentences.japanese: 今回の地震では、色々な場所で大きな被害が出ています。
sentences.english: This earthquake has caused significant damage in many places.

meaningMnemonic: The place you meet for deliberation in Japan is called the Diet . It's their version of congress .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: もう議会で決定したことなんだ。
sentences.english: The Diet has already come to a decision.

sentences.japanese: 私たちの出した意見書が、議会で可決されました。
sentences.english: The opinion letter we submitted was passed by the Assembly.

sentences.japanese: ウトウトする議員が多いので、議員たちは議会ではイスに座らず、立って議論することになりました。
sentences.english: Due to many lawmakers dozing off, members of the parliament have decided to stand and debate instead of sitting during sessions.

meaningMnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of difficult ? It's also difficult .
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: It's awfully difficult to load a cow into your Moo-zooka ( むずか ). Click. Boom!

sentences.japanese: それってそんなに難しいことなの？
sentences.english: Is that really so hard to do?

sentences.japanese: ちょっと私には難しそうだし、やめておくよ。
sentences.english: That sounds a little too difficult for me, so I'm not going to do it.

sentences.japanese: このゲーム、難しすぎて全然クリアできない。
sentences.english: This game is too difficult to clear.

meaningMnemonic: This is the noun form of disaster , so it means disaster or misfortune .
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: Think about how, the last time disaster struck, it was a wh ile ( わざわ ) before things got back to normal. Be careful of the い on the end, it can be tricky and make you think it's an adjective when it's a noun.

sentences.japanese: このお守りが、きっとあなたを災いから守ってくれるでしょう。
sentences.english: This amulet will surely protect you from disaster.

sentences.japanese: その人形が、この村に多くの災いをもたらしたんです。
sentences.english: That doll brought a lot of misfortune to this village.

sentences.japanese: 口は災いの元だよ。
sentences.english: The mouth is the source of calamity.

meaningMnemonic: You dislike someone so bad ly that it turns to disgust and hate .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You haven't learned this reading for 悪 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you: When you feel disgust for someone all you can manage to say when you see them is, " Oh ... ( お ), it's you." Feel the anger when you see their face, "Oh, you again. Bleh."

sentences.japanese: 彼女はいつも通り、私に嫌悪の目を向けてきた。
sentences.english: She looked at me with disgust, as usual.

sentences.japanese: ドラキュラはニンニクを嫌悪しています。
sentences.english: Dracula has an aversion to garlic.

sentences.japanese: もちろん嫌悪感を感じましたが、その時は何も言えませんでした。
sentences.english: Of course I felt disgusted, but I could not say anything at the time.

meaningMnemonic: You know the word 皿 (plate) and the word 洗う (to wash), right? You can probably guess dish washing is happening here, but this is a noun, so it's the idea of dishwashing , AKA doing dishes , or washing dishes .
readingMnemonic: The readings are the individual vocab words (you can tell because there's a bit of hiragana stuck on there). It's the reading for 皿 and 洗う combined.

sentences.japanese: レストランで皿洗いのバイトを始めました。
sentences.english: I started working part-time as a dishwasher in a restaurant.

sentences.japanese: 食事代は皿洗いでOKなラーメン屋さんがあるってテレビで見たんですけど、本当ですか？
sentences.english: I saw on TV that there is a ramen shop where you can pay for your meal by washing dishes, is this true?

sentences.japanese: リビングのソファで横になっている夫を横目に、たまりにたまったお皿の皿洗いをしているとき、とても悲しくなります。
sentences.english: While my husband is lying on the living room sofa, I feel really sad doing the piled-up dishes, stealing sideways glances at him.

meaningMnemonic: You know that 嫌 means dislike and this vocab word means the same thing: dislike or hate ! Though this word is an adjective in Japanese, it usually makes sense to translate it as a verb in English, because of the difference in sentence structure. However, a more literal translation would be dislikable or detestable .
readingMnemonic: Of all the things out there to dislike the thing I dislike the most is the killer ( きら ) of people. People should never kill people.

sentences.japanese: 私はピーマンが嫌いです。
sentences.english: I hate green peppers.

sentences.japanese: 僕には嫌いな人はいません。
sentences.english: I don't have anyone I don't like.

sentences.japanese: 色々とごめんね。俺のこと、嫌なやつと思ってるかもしれないけど、できれば嫌いにならないでほしいな。
sentences.english: I'm sorry for everything. I know you might think I'm a jerk, but please don't hate me if you can.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. The vocab has the added meanings of eww , gross , and even reluctant .
readingMnemonic: The reading for this word is pretty weird. It's different than the 嫌い word you will see in this level too. It is いや , so when you think of something you dislike, just think " iyah ( いや ), I dislike it." Also, think about that eww feeling it gives you when you think of the thing you dislike most.

sentences.japanese: それはゼッタイ嫌です。
sentences.english: I would hate to do that for sure.

sentences.japanese: 僕の彼女の嫌なところは、ポテトチップスにお湯を入れてマッシュポテトを作るとこかな。
sentences.english: My girlfriend's annoying habit is probably when she makes mashed potatoes by putting hot water in potato chips.

sentences.japanese: 仕事が嫌なら、やめたら？嫌なことを嫌々するのは体に良くないよ。
sentences.english: If you don't like your job, why don't you quit? It's not good for you to do something you don't want to do.

meaningMnemonic: Stand ing and enter ing are both 禁止 (prohibited). If you see this sign, it's essentially saying do not enter or no entry . While this type of sign will usually say 立入禁止 , you may also encounter variations such as 立ち入り禁止 or 立入り禁止 .
readingMnemonic: The reading for 立入 is a bit strange, but it might help you to know that it can also be written 立ち入り . The 立ち is the same one you learned with 立ち飲み and the 入り is the reading you learned with 入り口 . In our version of the word, the hiragana isn't visible (it's sort of pushed into the kanji), but the word is still pronounced the same way: たちいり . And 禁止 doesn't have any weirdness going on, so at least you have that!

sentences.japanese: スーパーのバックヤードは立入禁止です。
sentences.english: The backroom of the grocery store is off-limits.

sentences.japanese: このドアには、関係者以外立入禁止って書かれているよ。
sentences.english: This door says Authorized Personnel Only.

sentences.japanese: 立入禁止って聞くと入りたくなっちゃうのが人間でしょ？
sentences.english: When people hear that something is off-limits, they want to go in, don't they?

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
readingMnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: You're having this crazy dream . The dream allows you to do anything you want. Every time you ask "hey, can I do this?" The answer is always " you may " ( ゆめ ). Think of some things you'd want to do if you could do anything. Ask permission and get this answer in your imagination.

sentences.japanese: うわー、夢みたい！
sentences.english: Wow, it's like a dream come true!

sentences.japanese: 私の夢は日本に行って、日本で働くことです。
sentences.english: My dream is to go and work in Japan.

sentences.japanese: 昨日、コウイチに指圧をしてもらっている夢を見たんだ。
sentences.english: Yesterday, I had a dream that Koichi was giving me a shiatsu massage.

meaningMnemonic: An earth earthquake is just another way to say earthquake .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Notice that 地 is read as じ instead of ち . You've seen this happen a few times before, so just try to remember that this is the case here.

sentences.japanese: 最近、地震、多いよね。昨日もでしょ？
sentences.english: There have been a lot of earthquakes lately, haven't there? Yesterday too, right?

sentences.japanese: 人工地震って、本当にあると思いますか？
sentences.english: Do you think man-made earthquakes really exist?

sentences.japanese: 東日本大震災では、マグニチュード9の大地震が起こりました。
sentences.english: The Great East Japan Earthquake was a massive magnitude 9.0 earthquake.

meaningMnemonic: An earthquake disaster is just that, an earthquake disaster . These are no good.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 震災にあった日のことが、今でも忘れられないトラウマになっています。
sentences.english: I still can't forget the trauma I experienced from the day of the earthquake disaster.

sentences.japanese: 私の学校の先生は震災で帰らぬ人となりました。
sentences.english: A teacher at my school did not return home after the earthquake.

sentences.japanese: 震災で、地面が穴ぼこだらけになってしまいました。ここでは、震災から三ヶ月たった今でも、地面にヒビが入ったままです。

meaningMnemonic: One husband , many wives . This is polygamy . More specifically, 一夫多妻 is a term for polygyny , or marriage between one man and multiple women. Just note that 一 changes from いち to いっ , and 夫 changes from ふう to ぷ for some reason. You can remember this because you think people who practice polygamy should eat poo ( いっぷ ). meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. Something renews or gets renewed, or something changes. See? No direct object. Although it's not often translated as "renew," 改まる implies a kind of renewal in the changes it's used to describe — whether it's the revision of regulations or the old year changing over to a new one. It can also be used for personal improvements, or describe a shift to a more formal demeanor in social situations.
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You might remember this reading from the transitive verb 改める , but here's a mnemonic just in case: To be renewed means to be changed into something 新た ( あらた ). Out with the old, in with the 新た , right? Picture yourself in a situation where there's been a lot of change. Try to remember how it feels when everything is 新た . meaningMnemonic: Remember how 焼く is "to bake," "to burn something," or "to grill"? 焼ける is just the intransitive version. That means no direct object needed! Depending on the context, it can refer to anything from a muffin getting baked, fish being grilled, or pottery being fired. You can even use it when your skin gets a tan or a house burns down. Well, that last one is kinda sad. I hope it never happens. You can distinguish 焼ける from 焼く because when cooking, you always care ( ける ) to ensure the food gets baked or grilled really well. You want to make sure it's properly 焼ける 'd (heated through) to be safe!
